nodes.label: Carbon forms chains and rings via C-C bonds enabling organic diversity
nodes.objective: Explain why carbon can form a huge variety of compounds through chains and rings of C-C bonds.
essentialPoints: Carbon atoms can bond to other carbon atoms forming chains and rings
This gives rise to a very large variety of possible carbon compounds
Organic chemistry is the study of these carbon compounds

nodes.label: Crude oil: origin, finite resource, mixture of hydrocarbons
nodes.objective: Describe crude oil as a finite fossil resource formed from ancient biomass and consisting mainly of hydrocarbons.
essentialPoints: Crude oil is a finite resource found in rocks
It formed from the remains of ancient biomass (mainly plankton) buried in mud
Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, mostly hydrocarbons

nodes.label: Hydrocarbons: molecules of hydrogen and carbon only
nodes.objective: Define a hydrocarbon as a molecule containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms.
essentialPoints: A hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon atoms

nodes.label: Alkanes: general formula CnH2n+2 and first four members
nodes.objective: State the general formula for alkanes and name/recognise the first four members from formulae or diagrams.
essentialPoints: Alkanes are a homologous series with general formula CnH2n+2
The first four alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane
Alkanes can be represented as molecular formulae or displayed/skeletal structures

nodes.label: Building molecular models of alkanes
nodes.objective: Use molecular modelling kits to construct 3D representations of alkane molecules.
essentialPoints: Molecular models represent the 3D arrangement of atoms in alkanes
Building models helps visualise bonding around each carbon atom

nodes.label: Fractional distillation of crude oil (evaporation and condensation)
nodes.objective: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions using evaporation and condensation, based on differing boiling points.
essentialPoints: Crude oil is heated and vaporised then fed into a fractionating column with a temperature gradient
Hydrocarbons condense at different heights according to their boiling points, separating into fractions
Each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms

nodes.label: Fractions as fuels and petrochemical feedstock
nodes.objective: State that fractions from crude oil are processed into fuels (petrol, diesel, kerosene, heavy fuel oil, LPG) and feedstock for petrochemicals (solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents).
essentialPoints: Fractions are processed to make fuels such as petrol, diesel, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and LPG
Fractions also provide feedstock for the petrochemical industry to make solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents

nodes.label: Trends in boiling point, viscosity and flammability with molecular size
nodes.objective: Recall how boiling point, viscosity and flammability of hydrocarbons change as molecular size increases, and relate this to their use as fuels.
essentialPoints: Boiling point increases with increasing molecular size
Viscosity increases with increasing molecular size
Flammability decreases with increasing molecular size
These properties determine suitability of different fractions as fuels

nodes.label: Investigating properties of different hydrocarbons
nodes.objective: Carry out practical comparisons of viscosity, flammability and boiling point for hydrocarbon samples of different chain length.
essentialPoints: Compare viscosity by timing flow of samples
Compare flammability by testing ease of ignition
Compare boiling points using heating and thermometer readings

nodes.label: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons and balanced equations
nodes.objective: Write balanced equations for complete combustion of hydrocarbons producing carbon dioxide and water, understanding oxidation of carbon and hydrogen.
essentialPoints: Complete combustion oxidises carbon and hydrogen in the fuel
Products of complete combustion are carbon dioxide and water
Balanced symbol equations can be written for combustion given a hydrocarbon formula

nodes.label: Cracking: catalytic cracking and steam cracking
nodes.objective: Describe cracking as breaking down larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, and describe the general conditions for catalytic and steam cracking.
essentialPoints: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful molecules
Catalytic cracking uses a catalyst and high temperature
Steam cracking uses a high temperature and steam without a catalyst

nodes.label: Products of cracking: alkanes and alkenes; balancing cracking equations
nodes.objective: Identify that cracking produces both alkanes and alkenes and balance equations representing cracking reactions given formulae.
essentialPoints: Cracking produces smaller alkanes and alkenes from larger alkane molecules
Equations for cracking can be balanced given reactant and product formulae

nodes.label: Bromine water test for alkenes
nodes.objective: Recall that bromine water changes from orange to colourless in the presence of an alkene, used as a test for unsaturation.
essentialPoints: Bromine water is orange and turns colourless when shaken with an alkene
This distinguishes alkenes (unsaturated) from alkanes (saturated), which do not decolourise it

nodes.label: Usefulness of cracking: meeting fuel demand and supplying alkenes for chemicals
nodes.objective: Explain why cracking is useful, given high demand for small-molecule fuels and demand for alkenes for polymers and other chemicals.
essentialPoints: There is high demand for fuels with small molecules, more than crude oil naturally yields
Cracking converts less useful larger hydrocarbons into more useful smaller alkanes for fuel
Cracking produces alkenes used to manufacture polymers and other chemicals

nodes.label: Alkenes: general formula CnH2n and the C=C double bond
nodes.objective: State the general formula for alkenes, define unsaturation, and name/recognise the first four alkenes from formulae or diagrams.
essentialPoints: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
General formula for alkenes is CnH2n
Alkenes are unsaturated, having two fewer hydrogens than the corresponding alkane
First four alkenes are ethene, propene, butene and pentene

nodes.label: Functional groups determine characteristic reactions of organic compounds
nodes.objective: Explain that a functional group is a specific group of atoms responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of a compound.
essentialPoints: A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms within a molecule
Compounds with the same functional group show similar characteristic reactions

nodes.label: Combustion of alkenes: incomplete combustion and smoky flames
nodes.objective: Explain that alkenes burn with smoky flames in air due to incomplete combustion, unlike complete combustion of alkanes.
essentialPoints: Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion like other hydrocarbons
Alkenes tend to burn with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion
Incomplete combustion produces carbon (soot) as well as other products

nodes.label: Addition reactions of alkenes with hydrogen, water and halogens
nodes.objective: Describe the addition reactions and conditions for alkenes reacting with hydrogen, water and halogens, and draw displayed structural formulae of reactants and products.
essentialPoints: Addition reactions add atoms across the C=C double bond, converting it to a single bond
Hydrogenation: alkene + hydrogen (nickel catalyst) forms an alkane
Hydration: alkene + steam (acid catalyst, high temperature/pressure) forms an alcohol
Halogenation: alkene + halogen (room temperature) forms a dihaloalkane

nodes.label: Alcohols: functional group -OH and first four members
nodes.objective: Recognise alcohols by their -OH functional group and name/identify the first four members from formulae.
essentialPoints: Alcohols contain the functional group -OH
The first four alcohols are methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol

nodes.label: Reactions of alcohols: with sodium, combustion, dissolving in water, oxidation
nodes.objective: Describe what happens when alcohols react with sodium, burn in air, dissolve in water, and react with an oxidising agent.
essentialPoints: Alcohols react with sodium producing hydrogen gas and a metal alkoxide
Alcohols combust in air (complete combustion gives CO2 and water)
Alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions
Alcohols are oxidised by an oxidising agent to form carboxylic acids

nodes.label: Main uses of methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol
nodes.objective: Recall the main uses of the first four alcohols such as fuels and solvents.
essentialPoints: Alcohols are used as fuels
Alcohols are used as solvents (e.g. in inks, perfumes)
Ethanol is used in alcoholic drinks

nodes.label: Fermentation of sugar solutions using yeast to produce ethanol
nodes.objective: Describe the conditions required for fermentation of sugar solutions using yeast to produce aqueous ethanol.
essentialPoints: Fermentation uses yeast to convert sugar solution into ethanol and carbon dioxide
Requires warm temperature (around 25-40°C) and anaerobic conditions

nodes.label: Investigating reactions of alcohols
nodes.objective: Carry out practical investigation of alcohol reactions such as combustion or reaction with sodium.
essentialPoints: Safely react small quantities of alcohol with sodium and observe effervescence
Observe combustion of alcohols and compare flames

nodes.label: Carboxylic acids: functional group -COOH and first four members
nodes.objective: Recognise carboxylic acids by their -COOH functional group and name/identify the first four members from formulae.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids contain the functional group -COOH
The first four carboxylic acids are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid

nodes.label: Reactions of carboxylic acids: with carbonates, dissolving in water, reacting with alcohols
nodes.objective: Describe what happens when carboxylic acids react with carbonates, dissolve in water, and react with alcohols to form esters.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce carbon dioxide, water and a salt
Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce acidic solutions
Carboxylic acids react with alcohols (with an acid catalyst) to produce esters and water, e.g. ethanoic acid + ethanol forms ethyl ethanoate

nodes.label: Investigating reactions of carboxylic acids
nodes.objective: Carry out practical investigation of carboxylic acid reactions such as with carbonates or forming esters.
essentialPoints: React carboxylic acids with carbonates and observe gas produced
Prepare a small sample of ester and note characteristic smell under safe conditions

nodes.label: Carboxylic acids as weak acids: explanation via ionisation and pH (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids in terms of partial ionisation in aqueous solution and the resulting pH, relative to strong acids.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids only partially ionise in aqueous solution, releasing few H+ ions
This makes them weak acids with a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration
This links to the general concept of strong vs weak acids and ionisation

nodes.label: Addition polymerisation: monomers, polymers and repeating units
nodes.objective: Describe addition polymerisation as many alkene monomers joining to form a polymer with a repeating unit matching the monomer's atoms, and draw diagrams representing this.
essentialPoints: Addition polymerisation is when many small alkene molecules (monomers) join together to form one large molecule (polymer)
No other molecule is formed in addition polymerisation
The repeating unit contains the same atoms as the monomer, with the C=C becoming a single C-C bond
Diagrams can represent the polymer formed from a given alkene monomer, and vice versa

nodes.label: Using models to represent addition polymerisation
nodes.objective: Use physical or diagrammatic models to represent monomers joining into an addition polymer chain.
essentialPoints: Models can represent multiple monomer units linking to form a polymer chain
Models help visualise how the double bond opens to form single bonds linking units

nodes.label: Condensation polymerisation: two functional groups per monomer, small molecule loss (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain the basic principles of condensation polymerisation, involving monomers with two functional groups joining with loss of a small molecule such as water, using a diol and dicarboxylic acid example.
essentialPoints: Condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups each
Monomers join together, typically losing a small molecule such as water, forming condensation reactions
A diol (e.g. ethanediol) and a dicarboxylic acid (e.g. hexanedioic acid) can react to form a polyester
The repeating unit reflects both monomers linked by new bonds, unlike addition polymers

nodes.label: Using models to represent condensation polymerisation
nodes.objective: Use physical or diagrammatic models to represent two different monomers joining with loss of small molecules to form a condensation polymer.
essentialPoints: Models can show two different monomers each with two functional groups linking together
Models illustrate the small molecule (e.g. water) released during each linkage

nodes.label: Amino acids and condensation polymerisation to form polypeptides/proteins (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain that amino acids have two different functional groups and react by condensation polymerisation to form polypeptides, and that different amino acids combine to form proteins.
essentialPoints: Amino acids have two different functional groups in the same molecule (e.g. -NH2 and -COOH)
Amino acids react by condensation polymerisation to produce polypeptides
Different amino acids can combine in the same chain to produce proteins

nodes.label: DNA and other naturally occurring polymers
nodes.objective: Describe DNA as a polymer of nucleotide monomers forming a double helix, and name monomers of other naturally occurring polymers (proteins, starch, cellulose).
essentialPoints: DNA encodes genetic instructions and consists of two polymer chains made from four different nucleotide monomers in a double helix
Proteins are polymers made from amino acid monomers
Starch and cellulose are naturally occurring polymers made from sugar (glucose) monomers
